text: 66 Maja is a carbonaceous background asteroid located in the central regions of the asteroid belt, with a diameter of approximately 71 kilometers. It was discovered on 9 April 1861 by American astronomer Horace Tuttle at the Harvard College Observatory in Cambridge, Massachusetts, United States. The asteroid is named after Maia from Greek mythology, who is one of the Seven Sisters of the Pleiades and the mother of Hermes (Mercury), daughter of Atlas and Pleione. Maja belongs to the main belt's background population and orbits the Sun at a distance of 2.2–3.1 AU, completing one orbit every 4 years and 4 months (1,571 days) with a semi-major axis of 2.65 AU. Its orbit has an eccentricity of 0.17 and an inclination of 3° relative to the ecliptic. The observation arc for Maja begins at the Harvard Observatory, one night after its discovery. In the Tholen classification, Maja is a carbonaceous C-type asteroid, while in the SMASS classification, it is categorized as a "hydrated" carbonaceous subtype (Ch). Rotational lightcurves of Maja have been studied since 1988; analysis of a high-quality lightcurve by French amateur astronomers Maurice Audejean and Jérôme Caron from February 2011 yielded a rotation period of 9.73509 hours and a brightness amplitude of 0.25 magnitude (U=3). A modeled lightcurve from 2016, based on photometric data, confirmed a sidereal period of 9.73570 hours and identified two spin axes at (49.0°, −70.0°) and (225.0°, −68.0°) in ecliptic coordinates. Infrared surveys by IRAS, Akari, and NEOWISE indicate that Maja has a diameter between 62.87 and 82.28 kilometers and a surface albedo between 0.03 and 0.0759. The Collaborative Asteroid Lightcurve Link uses IRAS data, adopting an albedo of 0.0618 and a diameter of 71.82 kilometers based on an absolute magnitude of 9.36. The naming was proposed by Harvard's former president, J. Quincy, and officially cited in Paul Herget's *The Names of the Minor Planets* in 1955 (H 10). The asteroids 130 Elektra, 233 Asterope, and 1051 Merope were also named after the Seven Sisters, raising a minor concern in 1861 by George Phillips Bond, the observatory director, because these names were already used for some of the brightest stars in the Pleiades constellation in Taurus. As of now, no spacecraft has visited Maja. Although a flyby of Maja was initially planned for March 1997 during the Cassini–Huygens mission's departure from the inner solar system, delays in the launch—moved from April 1996 to October 1997—eliminated this possibility. Instead, Cassini-Huygens passed by asteroid 2685 Masursky on 23 January 2000.
